name: OPA365AIDBVR
title: 50 MHz zero-crossover rail-to-rail I/O CMOS operational amplifiers (OPA365 single, OPA2365 dual)
summary: OPA365 (single) and OPA2365 (dual) are CMOS op amps for 2.2 V to 5.5 V supplies with 50 MHz gain bandwidth and 25 V/µs slew rate. A zero-crossover input stage takes inputs 100 mV beyond both rails with no offset step, holding 100 dB minimum CMRR across that range, and the output swing comes within 10 mV of either rail. Noise is 4.5 nV/√Hz, bias current 0.2 pA and THD+N 0.0004%, which suits them to driving sampling ADCs, active filters and audio.

circuits.title: Fast-settling peak detector
circuits.description: Two OPA365s hold the highest voltage VIN has reached. U1 charges C1 through the BAT17 Schottky diode SD1 and R1; the diode stops C1 discharging back into U1 when VIN falls. U2 buffers the held voltage on C1 to VOUT. The loop around U1 is closed from VOUT through R2, so the diode's drop sits inside it, and C2 from U1's output to its inverting input keeps that loop stable.

circuits.title: Series resistor limiting input overdrive current
circuits.description: A unity-gain follower with 5 kΩ in series with its non-inverting input. When VIN goes past a supply rail, the input clamp diodes conduct and the resistor holds that current to 10 mA or less. The resistor adds thermal noise at the input, so in a low-noise design it is kept as small as the overdrive allows.

circuits.title: Follower with a series output resistor for capacitive loads
circuits.description: A unity-gain follower on a single supply drives a load of RL and CL in parallel through RS, 10 Ω to 20 Ω. RS cuts overshoot and ringing into large capacitance. It also forms a divider with RL: with RS = 20 Ω the error is about 0.2% into 10 kΩ and grows to 7.5% into 600 Ω.

circuits.title: Output swing to 0 V with a pull-down to a negative rail
circuits.description: A unity-gain follower on +5 V with its V- pin grounded. RP, 10 kΩ, runs from the output to a separate -5 V rail and pulls about 500 µA, which lets the output reach 0 V and a few millivolts below. Below that the output turns nonlinear and limits. Holding the output at 0 V trims the open-loop gain and the bandwidth a little, which matters for transient response and stability into a capacitive load.

circuits.title: Second-order Butterworth 500 kHz low-pass filter (multiple feedback)
circuits.description: A multiple-feedback low-pass stage on a single supply with a Butterworth (maximally flat) response, cutting off at 500 kHz and falling at -40 dB/decade above it. The output is inverted with respect to the input; an added inverting stage, a second MFB stage or a Sallen-Key filter gives a non-inverted output.

circuits.title: Three-pole 20 kHz Sallen-Key low-pass filter
circuits.description: A non-inverting three-pole low-pass filter at 20 kHz: an R1-C1 pole ahead of a unity-gain Sallen-Key pair (R2, R3, C2, C3) built round a follower, driven with 1 VRMS.

circuits.title: Inverting amplifier, gain -10, on ±1.5 V
circuits.description: Gain is -10 V/V, from R2 / R1, on split ±1.5 V supplies, so the output centres on 0 V. The non-inverting input is grounded and each supply pin has 100 nF to ground.

circuits.title: Inverting amplifier, gain -10, on a single 3 V supply
circuits.description: The same -10 V/V stage on +3 V with V- grounded. The non-inverting input and the input source's return sit at VCM = 1.5 V, so the output centres on 1.5 V; VCM may be any value inside the common-mode range, which reaches 100 mV past each rail.

circuits.title: Electret microphone preamplifier on 3.3 V
circuits.description: A single-supply non-inverting preamplifier for an electret microphone. A 4 kΩ / 6 kΩ divider from a clean 3.3 V rail biases the microphone and sets the amplifier's input common-mode voltage. Gain is set by 49 kΩ against 5 kΩ; the 1 µF in series with the 5 kΩ keeps the DC gain at one, so the output rests at the divider voltage.

circuits.title: Second-order 25 kHz Chebyshev low-pass filter, gain -5
circuits.description: An infinite-gain multiple-feedback low-pass filter designed for an inverting gain of 5 V/V, a 25 kHz cutoff and a second-order Chebyshev response with 3 dB of peaking in the passband. Gain is R4 / R1; the cutoff follows from R3, R4, C2 and C5. Its measured gain against frequency is the 25 kHz Chebyshev low-pass curve.

circuits.title: Unity-gain driver for a 16-bit 250 kSPS ADC (ADS8326)
circuits.description: A follower on +5 V buffers a 0 V to 4.096 V input into the ADS8326 through a 100 Ω / 1 nF network at the converter input; a REF3240 supplies the converter's 4.096 V reference. On a single supply the follower cannot reach true 0 V and a few codes near zero are lost. Where a -5 V rail exists, the optional network R2, C2 and a BAS40 Schottky makes about -0.3 V (a diode drop, -0.3 V to -0.7 V) for the V- pin, so the output reaches ground.

circuits.title: Inverting driver for a 16-bit 100 kSPS ADC (ADS8361) with a reduced full-scale range
circuits.description: An inverting unity-gain stage on +5 V referred to the ADS8361's 2.5 V reference output feeds the converter's -IN, while +IN sits at 2.5 V. R4 and R5 divide the 2.5 V reference down to 2.4 V for REF IN, so full scale becomes 4.8 VPP about 2.5 V and matches the amplifier's 0.1 V to 4.9 V linear swing; no negative supply is needed. The divider draws about 5 µA, inside the roughly ±10 µA the reference pin can supply, and its resistors need tight tolerance for the converter's gain accuracy. R3 and C2 filter and act as a charge reservoir for the converter's sampling capacitor.

circuits.title: Differential gain stage between the ADS1258 multiplexer and ADC (OPA2365)
circuits.description: Both halves of an OPA2365 on a single 5 V supply form a differential-in, differential-out gain stage between the ADS1258's multiplexer outputs and its ADC inputs, used with bridge sensors. Gain is 1 + 2·R2/R1, about 10 V/V; the two R2 must match closely for good common-mode rejection. A 2.2 nF capacitor across the ADC inputs takes the sampling current, and the 47 Ω resistors isolate the amplifier outputs from it. With bridges, ADC and reference on one 5 V supply the measurement is ratiometric; at the highest data rate with chopping on, the system gives 12 noise-free bits with 50 mV full scale.

circuits.title: Non-inverting amplifier with supply bypassing (layout example)
circuits.description: The OPA365 in the 8-pin SOIC as a non-inverting stage: VIN on +IN, RG from -IN to ground and RF from -IN to the output. A low-ESR 0.1 µF ceramic capacitor sits from each supply pin to ground, close to the part; on a single supply only the V+ capacitor is used. RF and RG sit next to -IN to keep parasitic capacitance there low.

operation.text: OPA365 is a single amplifier in SOT-23-5 or SOIC-8; OPA2365 is a dual in SOIC-8. Both are CMOS, specified from −40°C to +125°C, with identical specifications. Supply range is 2.2 V to 5.5 V; they offer 50 MHz gain bandwidth, 25 V/µs slew rate, 4.5 nV/√Hz noise at 100 kHz, 100 µV typical offset, 0.2 pA bias current and 0.0004% THD+N.
OPA365-Q1 and OPA2365-Q1 are AEC-Q100 automotive versions; OPA365-EP is an enhanced-product version for defense, aerospace and medical use.

The input stage has no complementary-pair handover, so offset does not jump partway through the common-mode range. The input range runs from 100 mV below V- to 100 mV above V+, and CMRR is 100 dB minimum over that whole range. The output swings to within 10 mV of each rail with a 10 kΩ load. Inside, a regulated charge pump raises the input stage supply to about VCC + 1.8 V.

Every pin has ESD protection; on the inputs and output these are steering diodes to the supply pins, which also clamp an overdriven input. Input current through them must stay at 10 mA or less; a series resistor at the input limits it, at the cost of its thermal noise.

At unity gain, a purely capacitive load of up to roughly 1 nF leaves the amplifier stable. Some very large capacitors (above 1 µF) have enough ESR to keep the loop stable. Higher closed-loop gain allows more load capacitance. A series output resistor of 10 Ω to 20 Ω extends the range at unity gain, with a gain error set by the divider it makes with any resistive load.

With light loading a CMOS output gets within millivolts of a rail but not onto it, and the gap grows with load current. A pull-down of about 500 µA from the output to a negative rail lets the output reach 0 V and a few millivolts below while V- stays at ground. This works on parts designed for it, such as these; with the output held at 0 V, gain and bandwidth of the open loop drop a little.
There is one mode. The amplifier works whenever the supply is above 2.2 V (±1.1 V); the maximum supply is 5.5 V (±2.75 V).
The amplifier runs from one supply or from split supplies. On a single supply, bias the input common-mode voltage anywhere inside the input range; that range reaches 100 mV past both rails.

Wide common-mode range, output swing to the rails, speed and absence of input crossover distortion make these amplifiers suited to driving ADC inputs with low THD across the full swing. An RC network between amplifier and converter both filters and acts as a charge reservoir for the converter's hold capacitor; its values may need tuning per converter.

The specified supply span is 2.2 V to 5.5 V, or ±1.1 V to ±2.75 V split; much of the specification applies across −40°C to +125°C. Figures that shift notably with supply or temperature are given as typical curves.

Place a low-ESR 0.1 µF ceramic capacitor from each supply pin to ground as close to the part as possible; one from V+ to ground suffices on a single supply. The output can deliver more than 65 mA, so low-impedance or fast capacitive loads draw large supply current; adding bigger bypass parts, for example 1 µF solid tantalum, helps dynamic performance.

Keep analog and digital grounds apart and mind where ground current flows; ground-plane layers spread heat and reduce EMI pickup. Route input traces away from supply and output traces, cross noisy traces at right angles if they must cross, and keep inputs short. Put RF and RG right at the inverting input. Guarding sensitive traces with a ring driven at low impedance cuts leakage from nearby traces. Clean the board after assembly; after a water-based wash, a 30-minute bake at 85°C drives moisture back out of the package.
